name: Bilal Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Bilal, and thanks for making time. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy plumbing fittings, copper pipe and boiler parts for Marlow & Pike, a builders' merchant on the ring road. I start at seven, check what sold overnight on the system, and place orders with about thirty suppliers, mostly by email now. Ms Okafor (my manager) signs off anything big. After six years I'm still the junior on the desk, so I get the tricky suppliers nobody else wants.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What has changed since the new owners came in?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like it when a delivery turns up right and the plumbers at the trade counter stop moaning. What wears me out is the pressure from head office. A private equity firm bought us two years ago and now every order gets questioned in a spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say it's another software upgrade, and we've had plenty of those. To friends I'd say the hype made a lot of people rich who didn't deserve it. Online I'd probably share a sarcastic article and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just between us, that's the easy one for me. I use an AI tool now and then to tidy up emails to suppliers, and it saves me ten minutes. The job would carry on, but the money would stay tight, which is the part that never goes away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am, and I'd keep using the email helper because it makes me look sharper in front of Ms Okafor. I'd also push my union rep to ask for the cost-of-living rise we were promised. That matters more to me than any software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels okay, if I'm honest. Not great, because there's nothing in the bank, but okay. Nothing is moving under me, so I can sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be borrowing from your son. What does a lost month look like at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Nadia does school-kitchen shifts, and her pay and mine just cover the bills. If either of us lost a month, we'd be borrowing from my son Idris, who is a nurse. I hate that thought more than any computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think the owners might use AI as an excuse even when it doesn't do much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the real risk in this one isn't AI. It's the owners deciding to cut the buying team anyway and blaming the software. Cutting costs doesn't need an excuse, but AI gives them a good one.

say: I'd say it's **another upgrade**, and we've had plenty of those.
I'd tell friends the hype made some people rich who didn't deserve it.
think: This is the **easy** one for me, because the job carries on.
The money still stays tight, and that **never goes away**.
do: **Keep** using the email helper, since it makes me look sharper to Ms Okafor.
**Push** my union rep to chase the promised cost-of-living rise.
feel: **Okay**, honestly, though not great with nothing in the bank.
S0.quote: The real risk in this one isn't AI. It's the owners deciding to cut the buying team anyway and blaming the software.
fieldNote: Steady about technology, already uses a little AI, so the plateau feels safe for his job.
He keeps pointing at the **owners**, not the tools, as the real source of risk.
Thin money is the quiet worry; the son's help is a last resort he dislikes.

steps.text: Keep using the AI email helper for supplier orders
Carry on buying plumbing parts from the same thirty suppliers
Ask my union rep to chase the promised cost-of-living rise

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say I'm willing to learn whatever they show me, as long as there's training time. To friends I'd say these changes are decided in boardrooms, and ordinary people carry the risk. Online I'd back anyone calling for a say for workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the buying desk shrinks from five to three within two years. I'm the junior, I'm 58, and Ms Okafor will keep the ones who can run the new software. I've been using an AI tool for months, which gives me a chance, but only a chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the free supplier-pricing course the merchants' association runs, and use the AI tool on real orders so I can show numbers. I'd join the union meeting properly instead of just paying my dues. And I'd start putting 80 a week aside, even if it means no holiday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a slow squeeze. I'm not panicking, because I can see some way to stay useful. But I'm tired of having to prove myself again at 58.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most, and what would you do about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The person I'd worry about is Ferdi, who sits next to me. He's 61 and still does half his orders by phone. If they cut the desk, he's first, and then me. I'd try to show him the email helper, even though it makes my own spot a bit weaker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your daughter Lena about her own job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say to my daughter Lena that she should stay in her teaching job. I'd tell her that anything involving people face to face is safer, and that I'll be fine, even if I'm not totally sure.

say: I'd tell my boss I'll learn whatever they show me, with **training time**.
I'd tell friends these decisions are made in boardrooms and **ordinary people** carry the risk.
think: I think the buying desk shrinks from five to **three** within two years.
Using AI already gives me a **chance**, but only a chance.
do: **Sign up** for the merchants' association pricing course.
**Use** the AI tool on real orders so I can show results.
**Put** 80 a week aside, even if there's no holiday.
feel: Like a **slow squeeze**, with some hope of staying useful.
S1.quote: I'm tired of having to prove myself again at 58.
fieldNote: He expects the desk to shrink and knows he is the junior; anxious but still planning.
Concern for **Ferdi** shows loyalty that works against his own interest.
Open to learning only if the firm gives time, which says something about trust in the owners.

steps.text: Sign up for the merchants' association supplier-pricing course
Go to the union meetings and not just pay my dues
Put 80 a week into savings and skip the summer holiday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's moving too fast and nobody voted for it. At work I'd say little, because the owners listen to numbers, not feelings. With friends I'd say the government needs to guarantee people an income, and quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my job is gone. Buying and checking orders is the kind of thinking work AI does well already. Two years gives me no time to start something new, and I don't have a cushion to carry me through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the union and ask what protections we'd get in writing. I'd cut everything extra, the streaming, the phone upgrade, the Saturday lunches out. And I'd check with the pension people about drawing early, even at a lower amount, so I'd have something coming in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels frightening, and it's the speed that gets me. I could manage a slow change, but this one feels like the floor has gone. I'd lie awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned living with your son Idris. What would be hardest about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My son Idris is a nurse and his work is safer for now, so I'd ask him whether we could share a home with him and his girlfriend for a year. I'd feel like I'd failed at being the dad who helps, but I'd do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first in the household, and what comes after?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What gets cut first is the car. I'd sell it and use the bus. Then the phone contract, then the gas heating, which I'd keep low to the bone. Nadia would say we need to eat first, and she'd be right.

say: I'd say it's moving **too fast** and nobody voted for it.
I'd tell friends the government must guarantee an **income**, quickly.
think: I think my job is **gone**, because buying and checking orders is thinking work.
Two years leaves **no time** to start something new without a cushion.
do: **Ask** the union what protections we'd get in writing.
**Cut** streaming, the phone upgrade and lunches out.
**Ask** about drawing my pension early, even at a lower amount.
feel: **Frightening**, because the speed is what gets me.
S2.quote: I could manage a slow change, but this one feels like the floor has gone. I'd lie awake doing sums.
fieldNote: Expects to lose his **job** and says why: thinking work, no cushion, two years.
His fallback is family, and shame about it is visible.
Sets out a concrete order of cuts, with his partner Nadia keeping food first.

steps.text: Ask the union what protections we'd get in writing
Sell the car and cancel streaming and the phone upgrade
Ask the pension office about drawing early at a lower amount
Ask my son Idris if we can share his home for a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short, but it can be used if people plan. At work I'd ask Ms Okafor to be straight with us about what happens to the buying desk. With friends I'd say we need retraining paid by employers, not by us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'd be pushed out around 2030, a year before it fully lands. I'd be 62 by then. What scares me is being too old to hire and too young for a proper pension, with a thin cushion in between.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the five years like a project. I'd get properly good with AI tools now, so I'm the one who runs them. In a couple of years I'd look at the trade counter or yard work, which robots reach later. And I'd put in extra shifts to build a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels manageable but heavy. If I behave well, there's a path. If I don't, there isn't. That's a lot to carry, at my age and with no money behind me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the extra years that you couldn't do in the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Nadia first. She'd want to stay put, and so would I, but I'd tell her I might move to counter work, even at lower pay. Working with my hands near the end seems better than being let go for good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you and Nadia decide about a move to counter work at lower pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The three years before robots catch up with hands-on work are a gift for people in the yard and at the counter. If it comes, I'd rather be standing in the warehouse than staring at an order screen that no longer needs me.

say: I'd ask Ms Okafor to be **straight** with us about the buying desk.
I'd tell friends that **employers**, not workers, should pay for retraining.
think: I think I'd be pushed out around **2030**, aged 62.
Too old to hire and too young for a proper pension scares me, with a **thin cushion**.
do: **Get** properly good with AI tools so I'm the one running them.
**Look** at trade counter or yard work within two years.
**Work** extra shifts to build a cushion.
feel: **Manageable but heavy**, because a path exists only if I act well.
S3.quote: I'd rather be standing in the warehouse than staring at an order screen that no longer needs me.
fieldNote: Five years makes him active; he plans a move to **hands-on** work to use the robot delay.
Stays at anxious because he thinks he'd be pushed out before 2031.
Clear on the age trap: too old to hire, too young for the full pension.

steps.text: Get good enough with AI tools to be the one running them
Ask about trade counter or yard work at Marlow & Pike
Take extra Saturday shifts to build a cushion

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a decent runway, but the owners won't use it unless pushed. At work I'd keep doing a good job. With friends I'd say we should start asking now what a fair deal looks like for people who lose work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be mostly fine. I'd be 68 in 2036, probably retired, so this one mainly hits Lena and Idris. My worry is the pension. If it doesn't keep up, I'd still be counting pennies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and build a cushion of three months in the first three years. I'd stay current with AI tools so I'm still useful until 65. And I'd talk with my kids about what to study, because ten years is enough time for them to pivot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels distant but not dull. I'm calmer than in the fast ones. Though I do feel a bit like a guest at a party that's about to end badly for other people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your son Idris about his career?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Idris wants to move from nursing into something more senior, I'd back him. Hands-on caring is safe a bit longer, and robots come three years after the thinking part anyway. I'd also tell Lena to keep her teaching job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does having ten years change what you'd actually do now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big difference with ten years is I can retire first. In the two-year picture I'd be thrown out. Here, with a little saving, I'd walk out on my own terms and leave the mess to the next group.

say: I'd say ten years is a **decent runway** but the owners won't use it unless pushed.
I'd tell friends to start asking what a **fair deal** looks like for those who lose work.
think: I'd be mostly fine, since I'd be **68** in 2036 and probably retired.
My worry is the **pension** not keeping up.
do: **Build** a cushion of three months within three years.
**Stay** current with AI tools so I'm useful until 65.
**Talk** to my kids about what to study.
feel: **Distant** but not dull, like a guest at a party about to end badly for others.
S4.quote: Here, with a little saving, I'd walk out on my own terms and leave the mess to the next group.
fieldNote: Ten years moves the problem past his working life; the concern shifts to his children.
The **pension** is the only thing that still bothers him.
His mood is lower than in the fast pictures but not calm, as money is still thin.

steps.text: Build a cushion of three months within three years
Keep up with the AI tools at work until I retire at 65
Talk with Idris and Lena about what to study and where to work

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. I'm 58, we're living pay cheque to pay cheque, and the market here has maybe two or three other firms that hire buyers. Two years is too short to change anything, and I'd be the first name on their list.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that people my age aren't lazy. We want to work, we've paid in all our lives, and what we need is a fair deal while things change. I'd ask the panel to say that to whoever decides.

headlineQuote: Two years is too short to change anything, and I'd be the first name on their list.
portrait: Bilal is 58, a junior buyer at **Marlow & Pike**, a builders' merchant, living with his partner on thin money.
He is **steady** with technology: he uses AI now and then and will learn more with training time.
He blames the **owners**, a private equity firm, more than the technology, and he leans on his union.
He grows **alarmed** as the date nears, and plans to use the robot delay by moving to counter work.
His real fear is the gap before his **pension** and the shame of leaning on his son.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture, because he'd be first on the owners' list with no cushion and no time.
whatWouldHelp: A fair **deal** for older workers in writing, paid retraining, and a pension he can draw on if let go.
